claim: The zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata) is a socially monogamous and colonial opportunistic breeder.
source: The zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata) is a socially monogamous and colonial opportunistic breeder with pronounced sexual differences in singing and plumage coloration.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of the species.

claim: The zebra finch has pronounced sexual differences in singing and plumage coloration.
source: The zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata) is a socially monogamous and colonial opportunistic breeder with pronounced sexual differences in singing and plumage coloration.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1 which displays male and female zebra finches with visible differences.

claim: The zebra finch is a model species for research into sex differences in vocal communication.
source: Its natural history has led to it becoming a model species for research into sex differences in vocal communication, as well as behavioral, neural and genomic studies of imitative auditory learning.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a research application of the species.

claim: The zebra finch is the most intensively studied species of bird that is maintained in captivity in large numbers despite not being a species bred for its meat or eggs.
source: The zebra finch Taeniopygia guttata is the most intensively studied species of bird that is maintained in captivity in large numbers despite not being a species bred for its meat or eggs, like the chicken or the quail (reviewed in Zann, 1996).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to Zann, 1996 as a review source.

claim: The zebra finch became popular as a pet bird in the 19th century because it bred well in captivity.
source: It became popular as a pet bird in the 19th century because it bred well in captivity, and was adopted for scientific study in the third quarter of the 20th century, initially for research into sexual behaviors (Morris, 1954; Immelmann, 1972).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to Morris, 1954 and Immelmann, 1972.

claim: The zebra finch was adopted for scientific study in the third quarter of the 20th century, initially for research into sexual behaviors.
source: It became popular as a pet bird in the 19th century because it bred well in captivity, and was adopted for scientific study in the third quarter of the 20th century, initially for research into sexual behaviors (Morris, 1954; Immelmann, 1972).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to Morris, 1954 and Immelmann, 1972.

claim: The zebra finch has been used in studies of the de novo evolution of vocal culture.
source: Later, the zebra finch was used in studies of the de novo evolution of vocal culture (e.g. Fehér et al., 2009; Diez and MacDougall-Shackleton, 2020)
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: The zebra finch has been used in studies of the neuroethology of imitative vocal learning.
source: the neuroethology of imitative vocal learning (Terpstra et al., 2004; Vallentin et al., 2016; Yanagihara and Yazaki-Sugiyama, 2019)
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: The zebra finch has been used in studies of the neural mechanisms of sensorimotor learning.
source: the neural mechanisms of sensorimotor learning (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2014; Okubo et al., 2015; Mackevicius et al., 2020; Sakata and Yazaki-Sugiyama, 2020)
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: Early acoustic experience affects song-based preferences of female mate choice in zebra finches.
source: the role of early acoustic experience on the song-based preferences of female mate choice (Riebel and Smallegange, 2003; Chen et al., 2017; Woolley, 2012; see the following video for a mating display in zebra finches: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TaC6D1cW1Hs).
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: Male zebra finches learn to copy and produce a tutor-like song.
source: Due to the pronounced sexual differences in singing and plumage coloration found in the zebra finch (Figure 1), earlier research quickly focused on when and how males learn to copy and produce a tutor(-like) song (e.g. Eales, 1987; Brainard and Doupe, 2002; Figure 2A)
evidence: Stated with citations and reference to Figure 2A showing the timeline of song development.

claim: Female zebra finches learn from their foster fathers to prefer particular male vocal displays.
source: and then eventually on how females learn from their (foster) fathers to prefer particular male vocal displays (Braaten and Reynolds, 1999; Riebel, 2000).
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: The zebra finch was the second avian species to have its genome sequenced, after the domestic fowl.
source: The zebra finch was the second avian species to have its genome sequenced (Warren et al., 2010), after the domestic fowl (Gallus gallus; International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004).
evidence: Stated with citations to the genome sequencing publications.

claim: The first generations of transgenic zebra finches became available following the appearance of transgenic lines of domestic fowl and Japanese quail.
source: Soon after the appearance of transgenic lines of domestic fowl and the Japanese quail Cortunix japonica (reviewed by Sato and Lansford, 2013), the first generations of transgenic zebra finches become available (e.g. Agate et al., 2009; Abe et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: Genome editing in developing zebra finches is feasible.
source: The proven feasibility of genome editing in both developing zebra finches (e.g. Ahmadiantehrani and London, 2017) and adult poultry (reviewed in Woodcock et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: The zebra finch may be used as both a basic and an applied biomedical model for development and for human health and disease.
source: means that this bird may also be used as both a basic and an applied (i.e., biomedical) model for development and for human health and disease (e.g. Han and Park, 2018; London, 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: Studies of zebra finch natural history in Australia have been essential to establish the rationale for studying this species as a model for acoustic communication.
source: Studies of zebra finch natural history in Australia have been essential to establish and confirm the rationale for studying this species as a model for acoustic communication (Zann, 1990; Elie et al., 2010)
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: The zebra finch exhibits extensive behavioral and physiological plasticity to withstand extreme temperatures of over 40°C.
source: For example, recent wild studies have revealed the zebra finch's extensive behavioral and physiological plasticity to withstand extreme temperatures of over 40°C (e.g. Cooper et al., 2020a; Cooper et al., 2020b; Funghi et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: The zebra finch is endemic to Australasia.
source: The zebra finch is endemic to Australasia, and evolved there as part of the Australian grass finch radiation within the Estrildidae (Olsson and Alström, 2020).
evidence: Stated with citation to Olsson and Alström, 2020.

claim: The zebra finch shares a common ancestor with Poephila finches, diverging around 2.9 million years ago.
source: The species shares a common ancestor with Poephila finches (long-tailed P. acuticauda; black-throated P. cincta; and masked finch P. personata), diverging around 2.9 million years ago (Singhal et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to Singhal et al., 2015.

claim: The zebra finch and the double-barred finch diverged around 3.5 million years ago.
source: Formerly, the zebra finch was placed in a genus with the double-barred finch (Taeniopygia bichenovii), but in fact these two lineages diverged around 3.5 million years ago (Singhal et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to Singhal et al., 2015.

claim: Two subspecies of the zebra finch are recognized: the continental Australian taxon (T. guttata castanotis) and the Timor zebra finch (T. g. guttata).
source: Two subspecies of the zebra finch are recognized, with the continental Australian taxon (T. guttata castanotis) having no clear genetic structure and apparently mating randomly within its breeding population (Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009). The other subspecies is the Timor zebra finch (T. g. guttata), found to the north of Australia.
evidence: Stated with citation to Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009.

claim: The continental Australian zebra finch taxon has no clear genetic structure and apparently mates randomly within its breeding population.
source: Two subspecies of the zebra finch are recognized, with the continental Australian taxon (T. guttata castanotis) having no clear genetic structure and apparently mating randomly within its breeding population (Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation to Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009.

claim: The Timor zebra finch colonized the Lesser Sunda Islands around 1 million years ago.
source: The genetic divergence between the two lineages suggests that the latter taxon colonized the Lesser Sunda Islands around 1 million years ago and has a reduced diversity and genetic distance driven by founding effects and selection, relative to the continental subspecies (Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation to Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009.

claim: The Timor zebra finch has reduced diversity and genetic distance driven by founding effects and selection, relative to the continental subspecies.
source: The genetic divergence between the two lineages suggests that the latter taxon colonized the Lesser Sunda Islands around 1 million years ago and has a reduced diversity and genetic distance driven by founding effects and selection, relative to the continental subspecies (Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation to Balakrishnan and Edwards, 2009.

claim: The insular subspecies of zebra finch differs from the continental Australian subspecies in morphological and behavioral traits, including song rate and mate choice.
source: The insular subspecies has also been occasionally studied in captivity, and it differs from the continental Australian subspecies in morphological and behavioral traits, including song rate and mate choice (Clayton, 1990; Clayton et al., 1991).
evidence: Stated with citations to Clayton, 1990 and Clayton et al., 1991.

claim: The two subspecies of zebra finch can readily hybridize and be back-crossed in captivity.
source: The two subspecies of the zebra finch are physically isolated from one another in the wild, but they can readily hybridize and be back-crossed in captivity to examine a range of questions in classical genetics and functional developmental biology.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: Zebra finches become sexually mature at between 90 and 100 days of age in captivity.
source: Zebra finches have a relatively short generation time for altricial birds (those that are underdeveloped at the time of hatching): they become sexually mature at between 90 and 100 days of age in captivity, at which point they are ready to form pair bonds, build nests, and breed (Zann, 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Zann, 1996.

claim: Zebra finches are highly social and can be kept at great densities in shared housing with a relative absence of highly antagonistic behaviors.
source: They are highly social and can be kept at great densities in shared housing with a relative absence of highly antagonistic behaviors.
evidence: Stated directly in the text with inference to wild behavior.

claim: Zebra finches congregate around food and water, and nest in close proximity in loose colonies for apparent social benefits.
source: This is likely to be related to the level of sociality and the highly fluid flock-wide social relationships seen in the wild (McCowan et al., 2015; Brandl et al., 2019a), as individuals congregate around food and water, and nest in close proximity in loose colonies for apparent social benefits (Brandl et al., 2019b).
evidence: Stated with citations to McCowan et al., 2015, Brandl et al., 2019a, and Brandl et al., 2019b.

claim: Zebra finches can successfully reproduce on a predominantly seed-based diet.
source: Provided with sufficient water, nesting sites, and nest materials, and one (or more) mate(s) of the opposite sex, zebra finches can successfully reproduce on a predominantly seed-based diet, simplifying husbandry, even during the nestling stage.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: Zebra finch clutch size is between 2 and 9 eggs with a mode of 5.
source: With a clutch size of between 2 and 9 eggs (mode: 5), and with brood reduction rates that can be less than 30%, each reproductive bout is typically rapid and productive.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: In the wild, zebra finches pair for life.
source: In the wild, zebra finches pair for life, and partners are found in close proximity during both the breeding and non-breeding periods (Mariette and Griffith, 2012; McCowan et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to Mariette and Griffith, 2012 and McCowan et al., 2015.

claim: In captivity, zebra finch singletons form pair bonds within days or weeks when introduced into a new cage or aviary.
source: In captivity, this strong pair bond is preceded by rapid pairing, with singletons forming pair bonds within days or weeks when introduced into a new cage or aviary (Rutstein et al., 2007; Campbell et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated with citations to Rutstein et al., 2007 and Campbell et al., 2009.

claim: Cross-fostering zebra finch chicks with Bengalese finches revealed that both visual and acoustic cues of social parents are learned during early development and used by young zebra finches of both sexes in mate preference following maturity.
source: For example, cross-fostering zebra finch chicks with the 'universal estrildid foster species', the Bengalese finch (Lonchura striata vars. domestica; Sonnemann and Sjölander, 1977), revealed that both visual and acoustic cues of social parents are learned during early development and used by young zebra finches of both sexes in mate preference following maturity (ten Cate, 1987; Campbell and Hauber, 2009; Verzijden et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Sexual imprinting in zebra finches occurs through a two-stage process.
source: This occurs through a two-stage process of sexual imprinting (ten Cate, 1985; ten Cate and Voss, 1999).
evidence: Stated with citations to ten Cate, 1985 and ten Cate and Voss, 1999.

claim: Neurophysiological, neuroanatomical, immediate-early gene, and transcriptomic analyses performed on zebra finch females reared in isolation or in the presence of a different songbird species confirmed the critical role of early life experience in generating adaptive responses to conspecific songs.
source: For instance, neurophysiological (Hauber et al., 2013), neuroanatomical (Lauay et al., 2005), immediate-early gene (Tomaszycki et al., 2006), and transcriptomic analyses (Louder et al., 2018) performed on zebra finch females that were reared either in isolation from any male birdsong or in the presence of a different songbird species have confirmed the critical role of early life experience in generating adaptive cognitive-behavioral (Price, 1979), neurogenomic (Louder et al., 2018) and neurophysiological (Moore and Woolley, 2019) responses to conspecific songs.
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Stress responses of formerly pair-bonded, but then separated captive zebra finches impact the epigenomic status of the birds.
source: Similarly, the known upregulation of stress responses of formerly pair-bonded, but then separated captive zebra finches (Remage-Healey et al., 2003), is also reported to impact the epigenomic status of similarly treated birds (George et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations to Remage-Healey et al., 2003 and George et al., 2020.

claim: When adult male zebra finches' RA- and Area X-projecting HVC neurons were experimentally ablated, only the RA-projecting neurons were regenerated.
source: For example, when adult male zebra finches' RA- (robust nucleus of the arcopallium) and Area X-projecting HVC neurons (Figure 2B) were experimentally ablated, only the RA-projecting neurons were regenerated (Scharff et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated with citation to Scharff et al., 2000 and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A new social environment may contribute to the diminished apoptosis of newly generated caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) neurons in the forebrains of adult zebra finches.
source: In turn, a new social environment (e.g. through the exposure to novel aviary mates: Barnea et al., 2006, and/or ongoing auditory experiences: Pytte et al., 2010) may also contribute to the diminished apoptosis of newly generated caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) neurons (Figure 2B) in the forebrains of adults.
evidence: Stated with citations to Barnea et al., 2006 and Pytte et al., 2010, and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Hair cell regeneration following a loud noise or antibiotic treatment in Bengalese and zebra finches occurs rapidly.
source: Second, hair cell regeneration following a loud noise or antibiotic treatment in both Bengalese (Woolley and Rubel, 2002) and zebra finches (Dooling and Dent, 2001) occurs rapidly, as it does in other, non-oscine birds (Stone and Rubel, 2000) and in some other vertebrate lineages (e.g. fish: Monroe et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Most populations of zebra finches in research laboratories around the world have been founded with birds held by aviculturists for over a hundred generations.
source: Most of the populations of zebra finches in research laboratories around the world have been founded with birds held by aviculturists for over a hundred generations (Zann, 1996; Griffith et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to Zann, 1996 and Griffith et al., 2017.

claim: Birds of domesticated zebra finch stocks are up to 30% larger in body size than their wild counterparts.
source: It has long been known that birds of the domesticated stocks are up to 30% larger in body size than their wild counterparts (Zann, 1996)
evidence: Stated with citation to Zann, 1996.

claim: Captive zebra finches are similar to their wild counterparts in respect to the genomic architecture underlying complex traits.
source: Captive birds are also similar to their wild counterparts in respect to the genomic architecture underlying complex traits (Kim et al., 2017; Knief et al., 2016; Knief et al., 2017a)
evidence: Stated with citations to Kim et al., 2017, Knief et al., 2016, and Knief et al., 2017a.

claim: There are known differences in linkage disequilibrium patterns within the genomes of captive and wild zebra finch populations.
source: although some caution still needs to be applied, for instance, to known differences in linkage disequilibrium patterns within the genomes of captive and wild populations (Knief et al., 2017b).
evidence: Stated with citation to Knief et al., 2017b.

claim: The zebra finch is an estrildid, a family that is endemic to the tropics and found across Africa, Southern Asia, and Australasia.
source: The zebra finch is an estrildid (Sorenson et al., 2004; Olsson and Alström, 2020), a family that is endemic to the tropics, and found across Africa, Southern Asia, and Australasia – with the whole lineage having evolved far from the ecological and evolutionary pressures of the temperate northern hemisphere.
evidence: Stated with citations to Sorenson et al., 2004 and Olsson and Alström, 2020.

claim: One of the almost ubiquitous characteristics of the estrildid family is the interseasonal strength of the socially monogamous pair-bond and biparental care for the young.
source: One of the almost ubiquitous characteristics of the estrildid family is the interseasonal strength of the socially monogamous pair-bond and biparental care for the young (Payne, 2010).
evidence: Stated with citation to Payne, 2010.

claim: Prior breeding experience enhances the success of subsequent breeding bouts by female zebra finches through increased output and shorter times between clutches.
source: Prior breeding experience enhances the success of subsequent breeding bouts by female zebra finches through increased output and shorter times between clutches, even when breeding with a new male in this otherwise lifetime pair-bonded species (Adkins-Regan and Tomaszycki, 2007; Smiley and Adkins-Regan, 2016; Hurley et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations to Adkins-Regan and Tomaszycki, 2007, Smiley and Adkins-Regan, 2016, and Hurley et al., 2020.

claim: Conspecific brood parasitism accounts for 5 to 11% of offspring in captive zebra finches.
source: Nevertheless, in socially housed groups, both conspecific brood parasitism – inducible by simulated nest predation in captivity (Shaw and Hauber, 2009) and accounting for 5 to 11% of offspring (Griffith et al., 2010)
evidence: Stated with citations to Shaw and Hauber, 2009 and Griffith et al., 2010.

claim: Extra-pair paternity accounts for around 30% of offspring in aviaries but is almost entirely absent in the wild (accounting for ~1% of offspring).
source: as well as extra-pair paternity – accounting for around 30% of offspring in aviaries (Forstmeier et al., 2011) – can partially confound social parentage, although extrapair paternity is almost entirely absent in the wild (accounting for ~1% of offspring; Griffith et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citations to Forstmeier et al., 2011 and Griffith et al., 2010.

claim: A comprehensive study found no evidence that either male or female zebra finches are targeting variation in individual quality when they choose a partner.
source: However, despite considerable variance in the reproductive success of individuals even in captive populations (Griffith et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), one of the most comprehensive studies examining the consequence of mate choice on fitness found no evidence that either males or females are targeting this variation in individual quality when they choose a partner (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to Griffith et al., 2017 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Adult zebra finches are likely to live between 3 and 5 years in the wild.
source: Since adult zebra finches are likely to live between 3 and 5 years in the wild (Zann, 1996)
evidence: Stated with citation to Zann, 1996.

claim: Zebra finches can breed continuously throughout the year if conditions are favorable.
source: and can breed continuously throughout the year if conditions are favorable (Griffith et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated with citation to Griffith et al., 2017.

claim: The strength of the pair bond in the wild zebra finch is seen in the expression of acoustic communication throughout the year, and high levels of coordinated duetting between the male and female.
source: Indeed, the strength of the pair bond in the wild zebra finch is seen in the expression of acoustic communication throughout the year, and high levels of coordinated duetting between the male and female (Elie et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citation to Elie et al., 2010.

claim: Close and regular vocal interaction between the members of a pair may play a role in individual vocal recognition in zebra finches.
source: This close, and regular vocal interaction between the members of a pair also perhaps plays a role in individual vocal recognition in this species (Levréro et al., 2009; Elie and Theunissen, 2018; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations to Levréro et al., 2009, Elie and Theunissen, 2018, and Yu et al., 2020.

claim: Highly coordinated acoustic interactions between female and male partners are a characteristic of the earliest passerine lineages as they had evolved in Australia.
source: Highly coordinated acoustic interactions between female and male partners are a characteristic of the earliest passerine lineages as they had evolved in Australia (Odom et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citation to Odom et al., 2014.

claim: The learning of adult male songs by juvenile zebra finches is particularly strong during early sensory periods, when embryos, nestlings, and juveniles likely form a sensory representation of the 'tutor song'.
source: The learning of adult male songs by juveniles is particularly strong during early sensory periods, when embryos (Antonson et al., 2021), nestlings (Rivera et al., 2019), and juveniles (Brainard and Doupe, 2000) likely form a sensory representation of the 'tutor song' (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated with citations to Antonson et al., 2021, Rivera et al., 2019, and Brainard and Doupe, 2000, and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Juvenile female zebra finches develop long-term song-type preferences used for mate choice based on early experiences with their own fathers.
source: Just as juvenile females develop long-term song-type preferences used for mate choice based on early experiences with their own fathers (Riebel, 2000; Chen et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated with citations to Riebel, 2000 and Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Young male zebra finches learn and then actively practice to produce songs that match their paternal (tutor) songs.
source: young males also learn and then actively practice to produce songs that match their paternal (tutor) songs (Tchernichovski et al., 2001; Figure 3).
evidence: Stated with citation to Tchernichovski et al., 2001 and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Tutors alter their song structure when singing near young tutees, which influences the song learning process for young zebra finches, analogous to humans changing their speech when speaking to infants.
source: Tutors even alter their song structure when singing near young tutees, which influences the song learning process for young zebra finches, analogous to humans changing their speech when speaking to infants (Chen et al., 2016; Carouso-Peck and Goldstein, 2019).
evidence: Stated with citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Carouso-Peck and Goldstein, 2019.

claim: The genetic make-up of individual zebra finches may contribute to the resulting song preferences and vocal production patterns through gene-by-environment interactions.
source: However, even in the case of strong social environmental impact upon song learning during the sensitive period, the genetic make-up of individuals may contribute to the resulting song preferences and vocal production patterns through gene-by-environment interactions (Mets and Brainard, 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Mets and Brainard, 2019.

claim: Male zebra finches preferentially learn to sing from song tutors of the same species over those of another species when given equal access.
source: Accordingly, in zebra finches, males preferentially learn to sing from song tutors of the same species over those of another species when given equal access (Clayton, 1988)
evidence: Stated with citation to Clayton, 1988.

claim: Both song-naïve and cross-fostered female zebra finches show greater neuronal spike rates in response to unfamiliar conspecific over an unfamiliar third species' songs.
source: and both song-naïve and cross-fostered females show greater neuronal spike rates in response to unfamiliar conspecific over an unfamiliar third species' songs (Hauber et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation to Hauber et al., 2013.

claim: The species-specific typical pattern of socially learned song structure can culturally evolve across just a handful of generations in initially naïve zebra finch populations.
source: Similarly, the species-specific typical pattern of socially learned song structure can culturally evolve across of just a handful of generations in initially naïve zebra finch populations (Fehér et al., 2009; Diez and MacDougall-Shackleton, 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations to Fehér et al., 2009 and Diez and MacDougall-Shackleton, 2020.

claim: In adulthood, male and female zebra finches can quickly memorize individual vocal characteristics and recognize the identity of others for at least a month without reinforcement.
source: In adulthood, male and female zebra finches can quickly memorize individual vocal characteristics and recognize the identity of others for at least a month without reinforcement (Yu et al., 2020)
evidence: Stated with citation to Yu et al., 2020.

claim: Experiences with other songs in adulthood do not affect the crystallized songs of male zebra finches.
source: However, experiences with other songs in adulthood do not affect the crystallized songs of males.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: Following the presentation of tape-recorded songs of conspecifics, the expression level of egr-1 (also known as ZENK) increases within the zebra finch auditory forebrain.
source: Accordingly, following the presentation of tape-recorded songs of conspecifics, the expression level of an immediate-early gene, egr-1 (also known as ZENK), which is associated with neural activation, increases within the zebra finch auditory forebrain, as found in other songbird species (Mello et al., 1992; Louder et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citations to Mello et al., 1992 and Louder et al., 2016.

claim: Neural responses within the NCM are selective for tutor songs.
source: Furthermore, neural responses within the NCM, a subregion of the auditory forebrain, are selective for tutor songs (Yanagihara and Yazaki-Sugiyama, 2016)
evidence: Stated with citation to Yanagihara and Yazaki-Sugiyama, 2016.

claim: Song-induced expression of ZENK positively correlates with the increased similarity of the bird's copied song to that of the tutor.
source: and song-induced expression of neural transcription factors (again, ZENK) also positively correlate with the increased similarity of the bird's copied song to that of the tutor (Bolhuis et al., 2000)
evidence: Stated with citation to Bolhuis et al., 2000.

claim: NCM lesions in adult male zebra finches reduce their ability to recognize songs, but not to produce them.
source: Accordingly, NCM lesions in adult male zebra finches reduce their ability to recognize songs, but not to produce them (Gobes and Bolhuis, 2007).
evidence: Stated with citation to Gobes and Bolhuis, 2007.

claim: Behavioral preferences for conspecific versus heterospecific songs in female zebra finches can be eliminated by damaging the CMM nucleus (caudomedial mesopallium).
source: In female zebra finches, on the other hand, behavioral preferences for conspecific versus heterospecific songs can be eliminated by damaging the nearby CMM nucleus (caudomedial mesopallium) (MacDougall-Shackleton et al., 1998).
evidence: Stated with citation to MacDougall-Shackleton et al., 1998.

claim: Juvenile male zebra finches mimic the tutor song while females only produce non-learned 'calls'.
source: Juvenile male zebra finches mimic the tutor song while females only produce non-learned 'calls' (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated directly in the text with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Several regions in the zebra finch brain associated with song production are dramatically larger in male zebra finches, a result of neurons in some of these regions atrophying in females while increasing in size and connections in males.
source: In turn, several regions in the zebra finch brain associated with song production are dramatically larger in male zebra finches, a result of neurons in some of these regions atrophying in females while increasing in size and connections in males (Figure 2B; Konishi and Akutagawa, 1985).
evidence: Stated with citation to Konishi and Akutagawa, 1985 and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Several brain regions in male zebra finches selectively respond to the 'bird's-own-song' in anesthetized males.
source: Several of these regions selectively respond to the 'bird's-own-song' in anesthetized males (Doupe and Konishi, 1991)
evidence: Stated with citation to Doupe and Konishi, 1991.

claim: Own-song specific auditory responses are gated by behavioral states and much less pronounced in awake birds.
source: however, the role of such own-song specific auditory responses is no longer clear, as they are gated by behavioral states (Hessler and Doupe, 1999) and much less pronounced in awake birds (Schmidt and Konishi, 1998).
evidence: Stated with citations to Hessler and Doupe, 1999 and Schmidt and Konishi, 1998.

claim: The premotor circuit for song production receives input from auditory nuclei via the HVC, which then projects to the RA, and subsequently connects to the brainstem motor nuclei and syrinx.
source: The premotor circuit for song production receives input from auditory nuclei via the HVC, which then projects to the RA, and subsequently connects to the brainstem motor nuclei and syrinx (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated directly in the text with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The motor pathway is crucial during the learning process to generate stereotyped adult songs.
source: This 'motor pathway' is crucial during the learning process (Aronov et al., 2008) to generate stereotyped adult songs (Simpson and Vicario, 1990).
evidence: Stated with citations to Aronov et al., 2008 and Simpson and Vicario, 1990.

claim: While singing, neurons in the HVC that connect to the RA perform time-locked bursts of firing, coincident with precise sequences during the song.
source: In turn, while singing, neurons in the HVC that connect to the robust nucleus of the arcopallium (RA) perform time-locked bursts of firing, coincident with precise sequences during the song (Hahnloser et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation to Hahnloser et al., 2002.

claim: HVC neurons ontogenetically shift their spike rates to become increasingly sparser while producing the male's song.
source: HVC neurons also ontogenetically shift their spike rates to become increasingly sparser while producing the male's song (Okubo et al., 2015)
evidence: Stated with citation to Okubo et al., 2015.

claim: The spike trains of RA neurons lock into the timing of song's note identity.
source: whereas the spike trains of RA neurons lock into the timing of song's note identity (Ac and Margoliash, 2008).
evidence: Stated with citation to Ac and Margoliash, 2008.

claim: Cooling the HVC, but not the RA, slows down the song without affecting its frequency content.
source: By altering the local temperature of specific brain nuclei, Long and Fee, 2008 demonstrated that the temporal match between HVC, but not RA, and the song's timing pattern is a causal link, as cooling the HVC, but not the RA, slows down the song without affecting its frequency content.
evidence: Stated with citation to Long and Fee, 2008.

claim: The anterior forebrain pathway (AFP) is required for vocal learning in juvenile male zebra finches, but not the production of stereotyped adult song.
source: By contrast, the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP), homologous to the mammalian basal ganglia–thalamocortical pathway, is required for vocal learning in juvenile male zebra finches, but not the production of stereotyped adult song (Bottjer et al., 1984).
evidence: Stated with citation to Bottjer et al., 1984.

claim: Area X and LMAN are involved in producing song variability in juvenile birds during vocal learning.
source: In this pathway, Area X and the lateral magnocellular nucleus of the anterior nidopallium (LMAN) are involved in producing song variability in juvenile birds during vocal learning (Woolley and Kao, 2015; Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated with citation to Woolley and Kao, 2015 and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Theoretical modelling and experimental studies have pointed to the critical role of vocal motor variability as the substrate upon which trial-and-error learning through reinforcement mechanisms may operate to shape vocal production ontogeny.
source: Specifically, both theoretical modelling (including in humans) and experimental studies of this pathway (in zebra finches) have pointed to the critical role of vocal motor variability as the substrate upon which trial-and-error learning through reinforcement mechanisms may operate to shape vocal production ontogeny (Dhawale et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to Dhawale et al., 2017.

claim: Inactivation of LMAN in young male zebra finches regresses experimentally induced, recently learned changes in the subjects' song pitch.
source: In turn, the AFP is also involved in auditory-feedback based acoustic correction signaling for the motor pathway, in that inactivation of LMAN in young male zebra finches regresses experimentally induced, recently learned changes in the subjects' song pitch (Andalman and Fee, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation to Andalman and Fee, 2009.

claim: Gene expression patterns, including genes associated with speech in humans such as FOXP2, are highly expressed in the anterior forebrain pathway during sensitive periods for song learning.
source: Finally, gene expression patterns, including genes associated with speech in humans such as the transcription factor FOXP2, are highly expressed in the anterior forebrain pathway during sensitive periods for song learning, indicating potential genetic parallels of vocal plasticity in birds and humans (Haesler, 2004; Pfenning et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citations to Haesler, 2004 and Pfenning et al., 2014.

claim: Auditory feedback is necessary for the development of song in juveniles and the maintenance of song in adult zebra finches.
source: Auditory feedback, in which self-uttered and self-heard vocalizations are compared to a memorized song pattern, is necessary for the development of song in juveniles and the maintenance of song in adult zebra finches (Price, 1979; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1992; Leonardo and Konishi, 1999).
evidence: Stated with citations to Price, 1979, Nordeen and Nordeen, 1992, and Leonardo and Konishi, 1999.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons of the VTA that project to the anterior forebrain pathway through Area X encode perceived errors in song performance from auditory feedback.
source: Dopaminergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) that project to the anterior forebrain pathway through Area X encode perceived errors in song performance from auditory feedback (Gadagkar et al., 2016; Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated with citation to Gadagkar et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The VTA receives error signals from auditory feedback through the AIV, which receives connections from the auditory forebrain.
source: The VTA receives error signals from auditory feedback through the AIV, which receives connections from the auditory forebrain (Kearney et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Kearney et al., 2019.

claim: Neurons within the auditory forebrain demonstrate sensitivity to errors in auditory feedback.
source: Furthermore, neurons within the auditory forebrain also demonstrate sensitivity to errors in auditory feedback (Keller and Hahnloser, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation to Keller and Hahnloser, 2009.

claim: An international consortium sequenced, assembled, and annotated the first zebra finch genome in 2010.
source: Then, in 2010 an international consortium sequenced, assembled, and annotated the first zebra finch genome (Warren et al., 2010), only the second avian genome presented.
evidence: Stated with citation to Warren et al., 2010.

claim: The first zebra finch genome revealed the sequences of over 17,000 predicted protein-coding genes, as well as many regulatory regions and non-coding RNAs.
source: This effort revealed the sequences of over 17,000 predicted protein-coding genes, as well as many regulatory regions and non-coding RNAs.
evidence: Stated directly in the text referring to the 2010 genome.

claim: The initial zebra finch genome helped researchers to identify and map the expression patterns of ~650 candidate genes within the brain of zebra finches, resulting in an online atlas database.
source: Furthermore, the initial genome helped researchers to identify and map the expression patterns of ~650 candidate genes within the brain of zebra finches, resulting in an online atlas database that provides an opportunity to link behavior, neuroanatomy, and molecular function (Lovell et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated with citation to Lovell et al., 2020.

claim: A recent high quality, second generation genome of the zebra finch improves the accuracy of the reference genome assembly and annotation.
source: A recent high quality, second generation genome of the zebra finch, presented as part of the Vertebrate Genomes Project, improves the accuracy of the reference genome assembly and annotation (Rhie et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated with citation to Rhie et al., 2021.

claim: Multi-electrode arrays can simultaneously record the activity of numerous neurons in awake and freely-behaving zebra finches.
source: Questions regarding the activity of specific neurons can now be tackled using multi-electrode arrays (e.g. Lim et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2018) or wireless neurotelemetry (Ma et al., 2020) able to simultaneously record the activity of numerous neurons in awake and freely-behaving birds.
evidence: Stated with citations to Lim et al., 2016, Tanaka et al., 2018, and Ma et al., 2020.

claim: Imaging the neural connections between distant brain regions is now possible with tissue clearing and light-sheet microscopy.
source: Imaging the neural connections between distant brain regions is now also possible with tissue clearing and light-sheet microscopy (Rocha et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation to Rocha et al., 2019.

claim: Existing or new gene constructs can be inserted into neonatal zebra finches via electroporation-based gene construct delivery to study the genetics of vocal learning.
source: Existing or new gene constructs can be inserted into neonatal (hatchling) zebra finches via electroporation-based gene construct delivery to study the genetics of vocal learning as songs are memorized, practiced, and first expressed by young males (Ahmadiantehrani and London, 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to Ahmadiantehrani and London, 2017.

claim: Viral constructs were developed to control the expression of FOXP2 in zebra finches.
source: Viral constructs were developed to control the expression of FOXP2 (e.g. Heston and White, 2015; Norton et al., 2019), which is expressed in the song control regions within the male zebra finch forebrain and associated with inherited speech and language disorder in humans (Fisher and Scharff, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citations to Heston and White, 2015, Norton et al., 2019, and Fisher and Scharff, 2009.

claim: Recent applications of viral constructs have enabled researchers to 'implant' artificial song memories into the zebra finch brain.
source: Recent applications of viral constructs have also enabled researchers to control neurons with light (optogenetics), such as 'implanting' artificial song memories into the zebra finch brain (Zhao et al., 2019)
evidence: Stated with citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: The utility of the zebra finch as a neurogenetic model laboratory species has been somewhat inhibited by the low success rate in the development of transgenic lines.
source: However, the utility of the zebra finch as a neurogenetic model laboratory species has been somewhat inhibited by the low success rate in the development of transgenic lines that would enable direct experimental modification of the gene expression patterns in the relevant vocal-production and vocal-perception circuits.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: The low success rate in developing transgenic zebra finch lines may be due to the unique immune function of oscine birds inhibiting full viral delivery of gene constructs.
source: This may be due to the unique immune function of oscine birds inhibiting full viral delivery of gene constructs (London, 2020).
evidence: Stated with citation to London, 2020.

claim: Lentiviral delivery of human Huntington's Disease genes into zebra finch lineages causally demonstrated reduced vocal imitation and output consistency as a result of the treatment.
source: Nevertheless, the last decade has already seen the successful innovation of lentiviral delivery (e.g. Norton et al., 2019) of, for example, human Huntington's Disease genes into zebra finch lineages, to causally demonstrate reduced vocal imitation and output consistency as a result of the treatment (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to Norton et al., 2019 and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: To date neither a TALEN nor a CRISPR/Cas9 vector-based gene editing approach has taken off in avian (chicken or songbird) lineages.
source: However, to date neither a TALEN nor a CRISPR/Cas9 vector-based gene editing approach has taken off in avian (chicken or songbird) lineages (Woodcock et al., 2017; but see Cooper et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to Woodcock et al., 2017 and Cooper et al., 2018.

claim: Female zebra finches only slowly and partially assumed a role in some of the earlier behavioral and developmental studies on sexual imprinting.
source: Female zebra finches only slowly and partially assumed a role in some of the earlier behavioral and developmental studies on sexual imprinting (e.g. Collins et al., 1994), but now maintain a co-lead position.
evidence: Stated with citation to Collins et al., 1994.

claim: Mate choice is mutual in zebra finches and females participate in the initial pair-bonding decisions, as well as in all aspects of collaborative biparental care.
source: This is because mate choice is mutual in this species and females participate in the ever-important initial pair-bonding decisions, as well as in all aspects of collaborative biparental care (Riebel, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citation to Riebel, 2009.

claim: Female zebra finches make a critical contribution to the phenotype of their offspring through their investments into eggs, and the care of dependent offspring.
source: As such, females make a critical contribution to the phenotype of their offspring through their investments into eggs, and the care of dependent offspring (Griffith and Buchanan, 2010b).
evidence: Stated with citation to Griffith and Buchanan, 2010b.

claim: Female visual and acoustic displays serve an important role in the development and fine-tuning of male vocalizations during sensitive periods.
source: It is becoming clear that female visual and acoustic displays serve an important role in the development and fine-tuning of male vocalizations during sensitive periods (Benichov et al., 2016; Carouso-Peck and Goldstein, 2019)
evidence: Stated with citations to Benichov et al., 2016 and Carouso-Peck and Goldstein, 2019.

claim: Male vocal and/or visual displays serve in the activation of auditory forebrain regions in adult female zebra finches.
source: and that male vocal and/or visual displays serve in the activation of auditory forebrain regions in adult females (Avey et al., 2005; Day et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citations to Avey et al., 2005 and Day et al., 2019.

claim: The reduced volume of the song control system that exists in the female zebra finch brain may enable plasticity in the vocal timing of calls in social interactions.
source: For example, the reduced volume of the song control system that exists in the female zebra finch brain is likely not at all vestigial (Shaughnessy et al., 2019) and may be even more functional than previously thought, enabling plasticity in the vocal timing of calls in social interactions (Benichov et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citations to Shaughnessy et al., 2019 and Benichov et al., 2016.

claim: Female and male parental vocal communication with embryos in ovo in the nest shape the functional neurogenomic responses of the embryos themselves.
source: In turn, female (and male) parental vocal communication with embryos in ovo in the nest have also been discovered to shape not only the functional neurogenomic responses of the embryos themselves (Rivera et al., 2019)
evidence: Stated with citation to Rivera et al., 2019.

claim: Parental vocal communication with embryos shapes the acoustic tutor choice of young male zebra finches.
source: but also the acoustic tutor choice of young male zebra finches (Katsis et al., 2018)
evidence: Stated with citation to Katsis et al., 2018.

claim: Parental vocal communication with embryos shapes adult behavioral phenotypes and reproductive success.
source: as well as adult behavioral phenotypes and reproductive success (Mariette and Buchanan, 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to Mariette and Buchanan, 2016.

claim: The behavioral, neurophysiological and gene-activational bases of perceptual learning of conspecific song features appear to be both species-specific in song-naïve female zebra finches and dependent on early social experience.
source: Finally, the behavioral, the neurophysiological and gene-activational bases of perceptual learning of conspecific song features appear to be both species-specific in song-naïve (mother-only parent raised) female zebra finches and dependent on early social experience with con- or cross-fostered heterospecific male songs (Hauber et al., 2013; Louder et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to Hauber et al., 2013 and Louder et al., 2018.

claim: Cross-fostered male zebra finches show an inability to copy the temporal pattern of heterospecific songs due to a lack of ontogenetic flexibility in the neurons that encode heterospecific song-gap perception within field L of the auditory forebrain.
source: In turn, cross-fostered males singing the foster species' song famously show an inability to copy the temporal pattern of heterospecific songs, discovered to be due to a lack of ontogenetic flexibility in the neurons that encode heterospecific song-gap (silent period between song bouts) perception again within field L of the auditory forebrain (Araki et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to Araki et al., 2016.

claim: The zebra finch was not originally brought into the laboratory as a model system, nor championed as such by early research pioneers.
source: The zebra finch was not originally brought into the laboratory as a model system, nor championed as such by early research pioneers.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: The zebra finch has been progressively adopted as a useful focus of study in an increasing set of research fields since the 1950s, largely due to its accessibility and the ease with which it can be held and bred in captivity.
source: From the 1950s onwards, the species has been progressively adopted as a useful focus of study in an increasing set of research fields, largely due to its accessibility and the ease with which it can be held and bred in captivity.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: The traits that have contributed to the zebra finch's utility as an avian laboratory model species set it aside from most other avian species.
source: It is important to be mindful that the traits that have contributed to its utility and adoption as 'the' avian laboratory model species for basic and biomedical research set it aside from most other avian species.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: The zebra finch evolved in an austral ecological setting that is profoundly different from those in the many geographic regions where most laboratory work takes place.
source: The zebra finch evolved in an austral ecological setting that is profoundly different from those in the many geographic regions where most of this laboratory work takes place.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: The zebra finch is the most widely researched laboratory songbird in the world because of its uniqueness.
source: The zebra finch is the most widely researched laboratory songbird in the world because of its uniqueness, and not as a result of any advocacy.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.
